🎯This Lesson’s Objectives▼ Expand
❓
Big Question
Today’s Wonder

The Lady Linnet mocks Gareth all the way from Camelot, yet by the end of the chapter she defends him. What can change a person’s mind about someone?

🎯
Objectives
By the end of this lesson…
📖Reading: I will read from “Then they came out of the forest…” to the end of “Sir Gareth, or the Knight of the Kitchen.”
🎭Character: I will tell which character changes in this chapter and which one stays the same, and name each kind.
🔤Words: I will learn five words: courteously, hospitably, besieged, homage, and rebuke.
🎼Evidence: I will set the Lady Linnet’s words in order and hear her song turn.
📝Writing: I will plan Quick Write 3: two knights, one quality.

In Tennyson’s long poem about Gareth, the damsel mocks him all through a wood. Here is how he answers her, twice.

Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1809–1892)
0:45
AI voice reading, not a recording of Tennyson. Photograph: Julia Margaret Cameron, 1865, public domain.
🖋️ Pen: tap the word that tells how Gareth answers her the first time.
Gareth and Lynette
Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1872) · Idylls of the King · “I Shall Assay”
Tennyson spells her Lynette and her sister Lyonors; our book says Linnet and Liones.
“Damsel,” Sir Gareth answered gently, “say Whate’er ye will, but whatsoe’er ye say, I leave not till I finish this fair quest, Or die therefore.” “Ay, wilt thou finish it? Sweet lord, how like a noble knight he talks! The listening rogue hath caught the manner of it. But, knave, anon thou shalt be met with, knave, And then by such a one that thou for all The kitchen brewis that was ever supt Shalt not once dare to look him in the face.” “I shall assay,” said Gareth with a smile That maddened her, and away she flashed again Down the long avenues of a boundless wood, And Gareth following was again beknaved.
whate’er / whatsoe’er: whatever · therefore: here, in the trying · rogue: a dishonest person · knave: a servant; also a rude word for a low person · anon: soon · brewis: broth with bread soaked in it · supt: eaten · assay: try · beknaved: called “knave” again

🔤 Words: The Linnet’s Song
The other five of this week’s ten words. Tap a card to hear it.
courteously
Politely and respectfully, with good manners.
“…and still you answer me courteously and depart not from my service.” Green, Sir Gareth, or the Knight of the Kitchen
hospitably
In a warm, generous way that welcomes guests.
“That night Sir Gareth and the Lady Linnet were entertained most hospitably by the Blue Knight…” Green, Sir Gareth, or the Knight of the Kitchen
besieged
Surrounded by an enemy so that no one can get in or out.
“…we are going to Castle Dangerous where my sister the Lady Liones is besieged.” Green, Sir Gareth, or the Knight of the Kitchen
homage
A public promise of loyalty and service to a lord or king.
“…and do homage to him, and say that the Knight of the Kitchen sent you.” Green, Sir Gareth, or the Knight of the Kitchen
rebuke
To speak sharply to someone about something they did wrong.
“But the Lady Linnet came and rebuked her sister…” Green, Sir Gareth, or the Knight of the Kitchen

Professor Lovelore

Good. Gareth ends the chapter just as he began it, patient and courteous. Linnet does not. She begins with insults and ends by asking his pardon and defending him to her own sister. That is a dynamic character.

    Professor Lovelore Before you write
    0:11
    An AI-generated character and voice.

    Type your answers here. Your work is saved and goes into your Week 3 Work PDF. First, three questions about the end of the chapter. Then plan your Quick Write.

    Part 1Chapter ThinkingComplete sentences, with details from the text.
    1. Linnet says, “Surely you must come of noble and gentle blood.” Why does she think good manners must mean noble birth? Does Gareth’s answer to her agree?
    2. The Lady Liones shuts the gate until he is “a noble knight of noble birth.” Once she knows his name she calls him “my preserver and my love.” What does Gareth’s answer to her show about what he values?
    3. Gareth sends the knights he spares to Camelot to say “the Knight of the Kitchen sent you.” Why use the kitchen name when he could use his own?

    Two knights, side by side: Sir Gawain and Gareth. Your plan has four boxes.
    1. One quality a good knight needs. Courtesy, patience, keeping your word, humility, or your own.

    📌 Watch how
    Theo’s plan
    6th Grade Scholar

    Quality: Keeping your word when it costs you.

    Gawain: He rides out to meet the Green Knight as he swore, but he hides the green lace and breaks the bargain to hand over everything he wins in the castle.

    Gareth: He promises King Arthur to finish Linnet’s adventure and will not turn back, however she mocks him.

    Claim: Gareth keeps his word more completely than Gawain does.

    One quality a good knight needs.
    One moment where Sir Gawain shows it, or fails to (“Sir Gawain and the Green Knight”).
    One moment where Gareth shows it (“Sir Gareth, or the Knight of the Kitchen”).
    My claim, with a comparing word: which knight shows more of it?
